newsitem.title: Tanzania: Christopher urges closure of Rwandan camps.
newsitem.headline: Christopher urges closure of Rwandan camps.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Friday it was safe for Hutu refugees to return to Rwanda and that their camps in Tanzania and Zaire should be closed.
"We believe it is time to close the camps closest to the Rwandan border that pose the greatest security threat," he told a news conference after talks with African leaders on Burundi and Rwanda.
In a written statement issued later, he asserted that the "refugees should be encouraged to return voluntarily to Rwanda" and the U.S. view is that most refugees "can now do so safely".

Christopher's comments were an endorsement of the minority Tutsi-dominated government in Rwanda, which says it is safe for the refugees to return. Christopher is the most senior U.S. official to address the refugee problem.
Where voluntary repatriations were not possible refugees "should be moved to camps further from the border", he said.

He spoke after meeting Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa, Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and former Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere, the international mediator on Burundi.
The African leaders are trying to end a civil war in Burundi that has taken at least 150,000 lives since October 1993 and encourage negotiations toward a political settlement there.
They also discussed with Christopher efforts to rebuild Rwanda after civil war and genocide in 1994.
Christopher, on a five-nation African tour, arrived from Ethiopia and leaves Arusha later for Cape Town, South Africa.

While in Arusha, he was to meet the new chief prosecutor of the U.N. war crimes tribunal, Justice Louise Arbour of Canada. Washington is giving the tribunal $650,000 in new aid to help prosecute mass rapes committed during the Rwandan genocide.
There are some two million Rwandan refugees -- mostly members of the majority Hutu ethnic group -- in camps in Tanzania and Zaire, on the border with Rwanda.

The refugees fled their homeland in 1994 following the assassination of Hutu President Juvenal Habyarimana. Most fear reprisals for the genocide if they go back to their homeland where a Tutsi-dominated army is in control.
Zaire wants the refugees forcefully repatriated and last year sent back 15,000 against their will. Tanzania also wants refugees to return home but has not yet forced them to do so.
At the news conference, Christopher urged both sides in Burundi to suspend hostilities and begin all-party negotiations.
Regional leaders imposed sanctions on Burundi after a July 25 coup by the Tutsi-led military ousted an interim power-sharing government with the main Hutu party.
In an effort to get the sanctions lifted, Major Pierre Buyoya, who seized power in the coup, announced last week he was reinstating parliament and allowing political parties to operate again.
Christopher called these moves encouraging and urged Hutu rebels to also take positive steps.
"The rebel groups must know that we expect them to choose dialogue as well. It is time for all sides to stop the killing and start talking," he said.

The United States is trying to organise a 10,000-member all- African military force to respond if Burundi erupts in a wave of genocide. Christopher said Tanzania has joined Mali and Ethiopia in offering troops for the force.
